title: From Channel Sounding to Ring Tracks
notes: Open with the ring as an ordinary object that can become a measurement instrument. The question for this session is how radio observations become trustworthy information about motion indoors. This is the first 90 minutes of the conference's 180-minute tutorial; the second part is practical work. Introduce the tutors without relying on the inconsistent affiliation text on the conference page. Tell the audience that the goal is to understand, configure and critique the measurements, then use them in an indoor-positioning experiment.

title: The last few metres are often indoors
notes: Start with a concrete scene: someone looking for shared lab equipment, a robot trying to rendezvous with a person, or a participant following an indoor route. The building creates a different propagation environment from open sky. We need a local coordinate frame, useful update rate and an uncertainty estimate. Invite a show of hands for people who have tried positioning inside a lab, hospital, warehouse or campus. Avoid claiming that every application needs centimetres or that one technology always wins. The floor plan is a conceptual illustration, not a measured deployment.

title: Location becomes valuable when it changes an action
notes: Use the three examples to show why tracking is an engineering requirement, not merely an attractive visualization. For asset retrieval, room-level location may be sufficient; for a spatial interaction, delay and consistency can matter more. A track supports analysis of route and dwell, but location data about people should be collected with clear purpose and consent. Ask the audience to name the error or delay that would change a decision in their own application. This makes later tradeoffs in airtime, filtering and geometry tangible.

title: A range is a constraint. A track is a history.
notes: Define an anchor as a node whose position is known in a shared coordinate frame. A single distance draws a circle in two dimensions, or a sphere in three. Several ranges constrain a point; repeated estimates plus a motion model form a track. Introduce a_i for anchor position and p for the target. Explain that the radio does not directly return a floor coordinate. Calibration, height, geometry and time alignment must be handled beyond the Bluetooth procedure. We will return to that chain after understanding the radio.

title: Our route from radio measurements to ring tracks
notes: We will spend most of our time on Channel Sounding: what is measured, how exchanges are organized and what invalidates a result. The short positioning bridge is enough to understand what the later practical exercise needs. The final section introduces the existing application and a repeatable experiment. Questions and prediction pauses are included in the timings. The appendix is optional and outside the 90-minute total. State that live hardware availability is not required to understand the first part.

title: SensWear: our open physical AI platform
notes: Introduce SensWear as a reusable physical AI platform: acquire signals from the physical world, interpret them locally or in an application, and use sensing or actuation to close a loop. The nRF54L15 is the Bluetooth-capable processor used for this tutorial's platform story. The IMU adds motion information and daughterboards make sensing and actuation configurable. Open source is the project model; the campaign page says public source publication is planned before launch, so avoid telling participants that every advertised repository is already published today. Use the full sensor kit photograph to identify the radio board, daughterboards, debug board and ring enclosure.

title: One electronic platform. Many physical roles.
notes: Explain the separation between electronics, modules and enclosure. A ring is the form factor used in the tutorial title, but does not define the entire platform. The same design idea supports a body-worn sensor, a module attached to an object, or a fixed node on a wall. Changing placement also changes the antenna environment; enclosure and body effects require measurement again. A module is not automatically a localization anchor: it becomes one when its position is surveyed and the appropriate firmware role is configured. Keep this introduction concise, then present the campaign follow-up.

title: Follow our SensWear campaign
notes: Invite participants to scan our QR code and follow the SensWear campaign. Explain what we will share: hardware releases, project progress and campaign updates. Give everyone a moment to open the page. Connect the invitation to the tutorial: we want participants to keep building and experimenting with the platform after the workshop.

title: How can two radios measure a distance?
notes: Transition from the hardware to the measurement problem. All the intuition in this section will feed directly into controls or plots in the application. Distinguish the Bluetooth standard's exchange and reporting from a particular vendor or host distance estimator. There is no universal accuracy number attached to simply selecting a Bluetooth version. Introduce the two complementary observables: packet timing and the phase of tones measured over multiple frequencies.

title: RTT is a nanosecond problem
notes: Interactive prediction: increase the turnaround while holding the distance fixed. The initiator's total elapsed time increases, but the corrected propagation time and range stay fixed. Then increase distance and observe the much smaller nanosecond change. At three metres, round-trip flight time is about 20.01 ns. A one-nanosecond error after subtraction creates about 0.15 m of range error. The application decodes time_difference in 0.5 ns units; quantization is not a promise of corresponding accuracy. Use exact c internally and rounded display values. This demonstration is a mathematical model, not captured hardware timing.

title: Try it: move the target, watch the phase
notes: Give the audience thirty seconds to predict the result of increasing distance. Move the slider from three to six metres; the unwrapped slope magnitude doubles and wrapped phase cycles faster. Toggle wrapped phase off to make the slope intuitive. Add the echo, which is a weaker path with four metres extra path length, and show curvature in the phase response and deviation of the simple slope estimate. Explain the assumptions used in this model: reciprocal static channel, no clock error, no measurement noise, and a complex two-way product. It illustrates sensitivity rather than predicting performance of the hardware.

title: Tiny frequency errors can become range bias
notes: The two tone observations do not occur at the same instant. Residual oscillator frequency difference rotates the combined phase during their separation. Since a fractional offset is proportional to RF frequency, the error can also tilt the fitted slope. Work through the numbers: c times 12e-6 times 69e-6 divided by two is about 0.124 m. The app explicitly says the reported-offset sign convention is not pinned down in its educational analysis and exposes a sign control. Do not claim the selected correction is universally correct. Distinguish measured offset, controller-reported compensation, and residual offset; avoid compensating twice.

title: Build a sequence from main mode and sub-mode
notes: Explain the six permitted non-Mode-0 combinations, grouped here into three rows. The app exposes exactly these choices. Mode zero is not selected as the main ranging mode. When a sub-mode exists, the minimum and maximum main-step counts bound the run before insertion. Actual counts are randomized within the rules. A main/sub sequence can continue across subevent boundaries while a new Mode-0 prefix appears at each subevent. The offline planner selects an illustrative cadence; it cannot predict the controller's exact random decisions. Have the audience read the small sequence aloud and identify what each step contributes.

title: Zoom in: procedure → event → subevent → step
notes: Start with the smallest unit: a step is an RF exchange with one mode on a channel. A subevent groups steps within a reserved time budget. Events organize subevents, and a procedure groups events into a ranging operation. Repeated procedures supply measurements over time. These are CS events; distinguish them from the ACL connection events that anchor scheduling and carry control or data transfer. The app offers separate views for connection, procedures, events and subevents, individual steps and channels. This nesting explains why changing one small timing parameter can affect a much larger schedule.

title: The useful tone is only part of the airtime
notes: Use the actual application screenshot as a preview of the detailed timing view. Zoom with the live app if the audience wants individual numbers. T_PM is the phase-measurement period, T_SW an antenna switching period, T_RD ramp-down, T_GD a guard, and T_IP1 or T_IP2 an interlude according to the mode. Frequency-change time is represented between steps in the event view. Longer phase measurement or more antenna paths expands the complete exchange, not merely the visually highlighted tone. The screenshot is an offline plan with explicit example assumptions and is not a captured over-the-air waveform.

title: Ranging rate has an airtime budget
notes: Label the arithmetic explicitly as an illustrative budget, not a benchmark of this firmware. Four sequential links consuming twenty milliseconds each already require eighty milliseconds, before other overhead; that gives an optimistic ceiling of 12.5 complete sweeps per second. Actual scheduling can be more complex, so measure it. The app visualizes an RAS reflector-data lane and compares its transfer with the next procedure. Connection interval and ATT MTU can matter for carrying results. More antennas, repeated channels or longer tone windows may improve observability but consume airtime. The sample app is principally pairwise; multi-anchor orchestration is a separate integration task.

title: Channels: coverage and coexistence
notes: The CS channel arrangement differs from the ordinary BLE data-channel grid. Within 2402–2480 MHz, seven reserved indices leave 72 permitted channels. The application can edit the channel map and overlays reference Wi-Fi bands for context. Its example random generator is deliberately not the CS security DRBG; the actual on-air sequence cannot be inferred from the offline example seed. Losing channels can reduce frequency coverage and complicate slope fitting. For ideal uniformly spaced 1 MHz samples, the nominal two-way phase ambiguity interval is c divided by two delta-f, about 150 m; this is not an operating-range guarantee and gaps can make unwrapping harder.

title: Antenna diversity creates paths, not extra anchors
notes: A path is a transmit/receive antenna pairing. Multiple paths offer diversity against poor orientation or fading, but do not automatically become independent surveyed anchors. The specification permits several antenna arrangements subject to implementation capability. The local repository includes an nRF54L15 Tag reflector with two switched antennas; do not assume that this Nordic Tag has the same antenna arrangement as a SensWear board. On a worn ring, the hand and body also change the RF environment. Keep path IDs in the dataset and test orientation, enclosure and mounting effects empirically.

title: Security checks and measurement quality answer different questions
notes: Explain security at a conceptual level rather than presenting this prototype as a secure-access product. Bluetooth CS includes mechanisms intended to reduce opportunities for range manipulation: protected setup, cryptographic randomization and packet/tone checks. RTT and PBR can supply complementary evidence. The exact protection depends on the chosen security level, supported features and how the application consumes indicators. NLOS bias is a propagation problem, not necessarily an attack. Likewise, an attacker can target a clean-looking estimate. Our educational app should be used to inspect observations and validity, not to certify access-control behavior.

title: Indoors, the shortest path may be the hardest to see
notes: Point to the direct path and a longer reflected path. The receiver sees a superposition of complex contributions, so phase can curve with frequency rather than follow a single line. If the direct path is suppressed, a dominant longer path can produce a persistent range bias. Averaging helps random noise but does not necessarily correct that bias. Other practical contributors include oscillator residuals, antenna delays, body shadowing and bad report pairing. The most useful teaching experiment is to change one condition—such as orientation or an obstacle—and compare the raw evidence before and after.

title: From raw observations to a defensible range
notes: Describe what the repository actually implements. Pairing uses configuration ID, start ACL event and procedure counter; steps are paired in their common order and mismatched channels are discarded. The selected antenna path and quality filter affect the PBR data used. RTT uses paired time differences, validity and packet-quality information; its mean and median summarize accepted steps. A low spread does not eliminate calibration bias. Check controller reports and missing or incomplete procedures. This is a transparent educational pipeline, not a claim that a simple fit has the multipath robustness of a production vendor estimator.

title: Prediction pause: which explanation survives?
notes: Allocate roughly forty seconds per question: brief individual prediction, a show of hands, then reveal the answer. Question one checks whether the timing subtraction is understood. Question two checks whether precision is being confused with accuracy. Question three prevents a particularly misleading interpretation of the planner. Keep this interactive even if the room is quiet by offering two possibilities and asking participants to explain their choice to a neighbour. These questions close the 53-minute Channel Sounding block, at minute 66.

title: Several ranges become a position estimate
notes: This is the bridge to the second part, not a statement that the desktop app contains a multilateration tab. Define the weighted nonlinear least-squares objective. The weights may reflect uncertainty or validated quality information, but raw quality labels are not automatically inverse variances. For a floor solution, account for anchor and target height: a radio range is three-dimensional, not automatically a horizontal distance. Either model height in the residual or project using justified heights. Three non-collinear anchors give an ideal two-dimensional solution; extra well-placed anchors help diagnose inconsistency and maintain coverage when one link fails. Outliers may require robust losses or rejection before solving.

title: Geometry can amplify the same range noise
notes: Toggle between four anchors surrounding the target and four clustered near one wall. The chart computes a local covariance from the range Jacobian and the assumed independent equal-variance range errors. The ellipse shows one-standard-deviation principal axes, not a guaranteed coverage boundary or measured accuracy. Clustered anchor bearings make at least one direction less observable. Explain that adding anchors close to one another can provide less benefit than improving spatial diversity. This local model excludes multipath bias and wrong surveyed coordinates. Ask where participants would mount the fourth anchor in their own room.

title: Tracking needs time, and evaluation needs truth
notes: A moving ring is not at the same point during every pairwise link. Attach timestamps and understand the age of each range before solving. Temporal filtering can reduce jitter but introduce delay and hide failures; compare filtered and unfiltered estimates. IMU measurements can extend the model, but inertial integration drifts and requires careful fusion. For evaluation, use labelled checkpoints or an independent reference trajectory. Report the median and a tail percentile such as the 95th, plus valid-fix availability and latency. Do not discard failed fixes from the story. Calibrate on separate data to avoid evaluating on what the estimator was tuned to.

title: SensWear makes the radio part of the experiment
notes: Return to SensWear with the conceptual pieces now in place. The tutorial deployment concept uses the ring as initiator and surveyed fixed devices as reflectors. The modular platform can also serve as a reflector or fixed node when equipped with the corresponding firmware. The role is not determined by whether a device looks like a ring. State the practical boundary: the supplied repository documents nRF54 development-kit and Tag targets; the exact SensWear board port and multi-anchor scheduling should be confirmed for the workshop build. The platform story is the path from the measurement to the wearable, not evidence that every proposed topology has been hardware-validated.

title: Mount for useful geometry—and repeatability
notes: Imagine four fixed SensWear-compatible nodes around the room or mounted on walls. Use a common coordinate frame and record heights. Leave the antenna clear of metal and document orientation and mounting material so the experiment can be repeated. Record firmware build, configuration, antenna selection and a physical anchor ID. Test known line-of-sight distances before adding movement and obstructions. A small coordinate survey error can look like a radio bias. Begin with one pair, then add anchors. If the intended wearable initiator build is not available, the documented DK-plus-reflector setup still supports the radio-learning exercises.

title: The lab question: what changes a range?
notes: Set up the second part as an experiment rather than a race to produce the prettiest track. Teams first collect a static known-distance baseline with a reproducible configuration and a consistent antenna reference point. Next, vary orientation or insert an obstacle while holding distance fixed. Finally, change an allowed schedule setting and assess the tradeoff between usable observations and update rate. Record enough context to explain differences. Use separate calibration and evaluation runs for later multilateration. If RF hardware fails, use the simulator for workflow training and a supplied real recording only if one is available; do not label synthetic data as a real fallback measurement set.

title: Bluetooth 6.0 adds a ranging primitive
notes: Position Channel Sounding within Bluetooth LE. It was introduced in Core 6.0. RSSI is a received-power measurement, not a time of flight. Direction Finding is a separate angle technique; do not equate its antenna array processing with Channel Sounding antenna paths. CS adds an interoperable way to exchange and report observations for ranging. A Bluetooth product label alone is insufficient: check the supported features and the firmware implementation on each side. The app also exposes newer options; the main lesson deliberately uses the Bluetooth 6.0 baseline with Inline PCT Transfer disabled.

title: Follow the complete measurement chain
notes: Walk through one pairwise experiment. The host requests a configuration that both controllers can support. The controller schedules time-critical RF exchanges; the host PC is not timing the radio. Results reach the application, including the peer's information where required. The analysis pairs corresponding reports and estimates a range. In this repository, configuration, wire protocol, results analysis and visualization are separate components. That separation is educational: an unexpected range can be traced backward to a configuration, a timing choice or the raw step observations.

title: Two observables, different sensitivities
notes: Preview the two measurement principles before deriving them. RTT cares about extremely small differences between timing intervals; PBR turns variation over frequency into delay. PBR is attractive for fine ranging, but phase ambiguity and multipath matter. RTT provides a complementary check and participates in security designs. The app's separate mean, median and slope traces make these distinctions visible; they are not a mandated Bluetooth fusion algorithm. Ask the audience which observable they expect to change when the reflector processing delay changes.

title: RTT: remove the time spent inside the reflector
notes: Read the four timestamps in order. The initiator measures t4 minus t1 on its clock. The reflector measures t3 minus t2 on its own clock. Subtracting the turnaround removes the time when a signal was not in flight. Divide the remaining round trip by two, then multiply by propagation speed. This model assumes reciprocal propagation and compatible calibrated time scales; it does not require comparing absolute clock epochs. Real implementations also address frequency offset, timestamp bias and packet quality. Host arrival timestamps are not substitutes for controller measurements.

title: Phase tells us where we are in a cycle
notes: Explain frequency, wavelength and phase using the plotted sinusoid. Frequency is cycles per second, wavelength is the spatial length of a cycle, and phase is position within that cycle. A receiver has a local oscillator; measured phase is relative to that reference. We cannot infer a unique metre-scale distance from the fractional position within one radio cycle. The plot is a spatial teaching sketch, not an oscilloscope trace from the application. Introduce radians now so the later slope equation has familiar units.

title: One frequency leaves many possible distances
notes: Separate single-tone ambiguity from the wider ambiguity associated with frequency spacing. Because the propagation path is counted twice, increasing the one-way distance by half a wavelength adds one full phase turn. A single phase angle cannot tell us which cycle we are on. Sweeping frequencies changes the accumulated phase at a rate related to distance. This is why Channel Sounding gathers observations over multiple RF channels. Absolute starting phase, hardware bias and oscillator offsets are additional reasons to work with a compensated two-way measurement instead of a single receive phase.

title: Pair the two phase observations
notes: Use complex notation only as much as needed: z equals I plus jQ, and its angle is the measured phase. In the conventional two-way exchange, combining matched phase observations cancels the opposing initial oscillator phase terms under the model assumptions. The application's baseline computes the complex product, not the conjugate product. The minus sign follows its receive-phase convention; other conventions may flip the sign. Residual frequency error and hardware effects remain. Peer data are therefore needed for this baseline analysis. Inline PCT Transfer is a newer extension with a different data path and is kept out of this baseline derivation.

title: Distance is the slope across frequency
notes: Differentiate the ideal phase model with respect to frequency. The intercept drops out, leaving minus four pi times range divided by c. The app groups repeated observations by channel, averages complex products for a chosen antenna path, unwraps the phases and fits a line. Do not average wrapped angles arithmetically. Fitting across more well-spaced frequencies can help constrain the slope, but it does not guarantee removal of reflected paths. Explain that sign conventions must be consistent through data decoding, correction and range estimation; avoid silently taking an absolute value to hide a sign error.

title: Four step modes, four clear purposes
notes: Present the four mode numbers as a map for the following slides. These are modes of individual steps inside a procedure, not four unrelated applications. Mode zero supplies calibration information rather than an independent distance estimate. Mode one is packet timing. Mode two is tone phase. Mode three contains both types of activity. A procedure contains a Mode-0 prefix and ranging steps; supported modes and combinations still have to be checked against controller capabilities.

title: Mode 0: establish the frequency reference
notes: Use the exchange diagram to show the initiator packet, reflector response and frequency-measurement tone. Fractional Frequency Offset describes the frequency difference relevant to the exchange. Fractional Frequency Offset Actuation Error characterizes how accurately a radio realizes an intended frequency; its table is a distinct calibration input. Do not call Mode 0 a measurement of the floor distance. In the app, the Mode 0 / FFO tab plots measured offsets and reported compensation over time. The conceptual diagram deliberately omits guard and ramp durations; the individual-step planner provides the detailed timing view.

title: Mode 1: timestamp the packet exchange
notes: Connect this mode directly to the four-timestamp derivation. The CS_SYNC structure and RTT sequence choice affect what is transmitted and the airtime. The application pairs timing data from both devices, then applies validity and packet-quality criteria. Timestamp unit size is different from empirical range accuracy. In the practical session, begin by inspecting the RTT tab and the accepted-pair count before interpreting the mean or median.

title: Mode 2: sample phase on each antenna path
notes: The initiator transmits tones and the reflector measures phase; the roles then reverse. The selected antenna configuration defines the paths, and each path needs a well-defined measurement slot. The planner includes switching periods and an extension slot, including reserved duration when a transmission is absent. The app excludes that extension slot from normal antenna-path measurements. Keep path identity when combining and comparing phase; different paths can have different hardware bias and propagation.

title: Mode 3: combine timing and phase in one step
notes: Walk through the exact conceptual order used in the planner: initiator synchronization packet followed by its tones, turnaround, reflector tones followed by its synchronization packet. Guard periods are not drawn here. Mode three is not a promise that adding two estimators produces perfect ranging, and the host does not automatically implement a robust fused estimator simply because both traces are available. It provides a convenient way to examine timing and phase evidence from related exchanges, at a different airtime cost from tone-only steps.

title: Appendix · the phase model in one place
notes: Use only for a derivation question. The alias interval refers to ideal uniform frequency spacing and the two-way phase model, not the guaranteed measurement range. Irregular channel gaps, wrapped phase, noise and multipath complicate estimation. The application is intentionally simple and provides intermediate plots to expose these limits. Frequency in the slope equation must be in hertz, phase in radians and c in metres per second.

title: Appendix · documented hardware routes
notes: Keep the nRF54LM20 DK, nRF54L15 DK, Nordic nRF54L15 Tag and SensWear platform distinct. The Tag's two-antenna RF switch is a documented board-specific feature. RTT in the debug/logging column means SEGGER Real Time Transfer, not round-trip-time ranging. The exact wearable build, power arrangement and peer set should be smoke-tested before the workshop. The repository does not lock an SDK west manifest, so match the documented SDK and toolchain across builds.

title: Appendix · a stalled run has a next diagnostic step
notes: Use as an instructor reference during the hands-on session. Begin with observable state rather than changing several settings simultaneously. A command timeout can close the app transport to avoid confusing a late reply with another command; reconnect to inspect the actual client state. If the UI is unresponsive, preserve any saved capture and reduce live analysis work before diagnosing RF issues. Do not treat a simulator run or successful firmware build as hardware verification.

title: Appendix · later Bluetooth features stay explicit
notes: This slide avoids mixing specification versions. The application help references Core 6.3, while some planner details cite Core 6.1. Its IPT option changes reflector tone behavior and switching timing. In that mode, the initiator can receive a two-way phase contribution through the modified exchange, and the app has specialized validation and initiator-only analysis behavior. These are not assumed in the Bluetooth 6.0 baseline derivation. Consult the app's IPT technical note and the relevant current standard before enabling it.
